summary: This standards-track document describes elliptic curve key exchange algorithms for TLS, in particular ephemeral ECDH key agreement and the use of ECDSA in the handshake, for TLS 1.2 and earlier. It was later replaced by RFC 9846.

plainLanguage.summary: This document adds elliptic curve cryptography to TLS 1.2 and earlier. It defines three ways for the two ends to agree a shared secret on a curve, two handshake extensions that let a client say which curves it can use, and the rules for the messages that carry the curve data. It also retires most of the old curve list, leaving five in use.

questions: how does tls use elliptic curve cryptography
what is the tls supported groups extension
subtitle: How a TLS handshake can agree a shared secret on an elliptic curve, and sign the agreement to prove who is talking.

tldr.problem: TLS needed a way to use elliptic curve cryptography, and the previous document on the subject carried a registry of 25 curves of which only three were in wide use, and still allowed explicit and deprecated point formats.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three key exchange algorithms built on ephemeral ECDH, two TLS extensions for negotiating curves and point formats, the data structures the handshake messages carry, and the cipher suites that name them.
tldr.outcome: The registry is trimmed to five curves, the point format is fixed to the uncompressed one, and public key validation is made mandatory. RFC 8422 was obsoleted by RFC 9846.

today: RFC 8422 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 9846. It was updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 10015.

sections.title: What This Document Adds to TLS
sections.content:
The document describes additions to TLS to support elliptic curve cryptography that are applicable to TLS versions 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2. The use of ECC in TLS 1.3 is defined separately and is explicitly out of scope. In particular, the document defines the use of the ECDHE key agreement scheme with ephemeral keys to establish the TLS premaster secret, and the use of ECDSA and EdDSA signatures for authentication of TLS peers.

The document is organised so that Section 2 gives an overview of the ECC-based key exchange algorithms, Section 3 describes the use of ECC certificates for client authentication, Section 4 presents the TLS extensions that let a client negotiate specific curves and point formats, Section 5 specifies the data structures needed for an ECC-based handshake and their encoding in TLS messages, Section 6 defines the ECC-based cipher suites and identifies a small subset as recommended for all implementations, Section 8 discusses security considerations and Section 9 describes IANA considerations for the name spaces created by the predecessor document. An appendix gives the differences from RFC 4492, which this one replaces.

Implementation requires familiarity with TLS, TLS extensions and ECC. The key words in the document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.
sections.plainLanguage: The scope is TLS 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 only, because TLS 1.3 does its own thing. The document covers the key agreement, the signatures that authenticate it, the extensions that negotiate the curve, the message formats, and the list of named cipher suites that pick a combination.

sections.title: The Three Key Exchange Algorithms
sections.content:
The document defines three new ECC-based key exchange algorithms for TLS. All of them use ephemeral ECDH to compute the TLS premaster secret, and they differ only in the mechanism, if any, used to authenticate them. The derivation of the TLS master secret from the premaster secret, and the subsequent generation of bulk encryption and MAC keys and initialisation vectors, is independent of the key exchange algorithm and is not impacted by the introduction of ECC. All of these key exchange algorithms provide forward secrecy if and only if fresh ephemeral keys are generated and used, and also destroyed after use.

In ECDHE_ECDSA, the server's certificate MUST contain an ECDSA- or EdDSA-capable public key. The server sends its ephemeral ECDH public key and a specification of the corresponding curve in the ServerKeyExchange message, and these parameters MUST be signed with ECDSA or EdDSA using the private key corresponding to the public key in the server's certificate. The client generates an ECDH key pair on the same curve as the server's ephemeral key and sends its public key in the ClientKeyExchange message, and both client and server perform an ECDH operation and use the resultant shared secret as the premaster secret.

ECDHE_RSA is the same as ECDHE_ECDSA except that the server's certificate MUST contain an RSA public key authorised for signing, and the signature in the ServerKeyExchange message must be computed with the corresponding RSA private key. With ECDHE_RSA a server can reuse its existing RSA certificate and easily comply with a constrained client's elliptic curve preferences. The computational cost incurred by a server is higher for ECDHE_RSA than for the traditional RSA key exchange, which does not provide forward secrecy.

ECDH_anon does not provide authentication of the server or the client, and is subject to man-in-the-middle attacks, so applications using it SHOULD provide authentication by other means. Despite the name beginning with ECDH_ rather than ECDHE_, the key used is ephemeral just like the key in ECDHE_RSA and ECDHE_ECDSA. In this algorithm the server's Certificate, the CertificateRequest, the client's Certificate and the CertificateVerify messages MUST NOT be sent. The server sends an ephemeral ECDH public key and the curve specification, unsigned, and the client responds with its own public key.

The document also lifts a restriction: it imposes no restrictions on the signature schemes used anywhere in the certificate chain, a restriction that the previous version of the document required and that originated in earlier TLS versions.
sections.plainLanguage: All three algorithms do the same arithmetic: each side makes a throwaway key pair, sends one half, and both sides compute the same shared secret. They differ only in how they prove who they are. Two of them sign the exchange with a certificate; the third does not sign at all, which is why the RFC warns about man-in-the-middle attacks there.

sections.title: Extensions for Curves and Point Formats
sections.content:
Two TLS extensions are defined: the Supported Elliptic Curves Extension and the Supported Point Formats Extension. These allow negotiating the use of specific curves and point formats during a handshake starting a new session, and are especially relevant for constrained clients that may support only a limited number of curves or point formats. The client enumerates the curves it supports and the point formats it can parse by including the appropriate extensions in its ClientHello message, and the server similarly enumerates the point formats it can parse in its ServerHello message.

A TLS client that proposes ECC cipher suites in its ClientHello SHOULD include these extensions. Servers implementing ECC cipher suites MUST support them, and when a client uses them, servers MUST NOT negotiate an ECC cipher suite unless they can complete the handshake while respecting the client's choice of curves. This eliminates the possibility that a negotiated ECC handshake is later aborted because the client cannot deal with the server's key. The client MUST NOT include these extensions if it does not propose any ECC cipher suites, and a client that does propose them may choose not to include the extensions, in which case the server is free to choose any of the curves or point formats. In the case of session resumption, the server simply ignores both extensions, since they only play a role during handshakes negotiating a new session.

The two extension types are added to ExtensionType as elliptic_curves(10) and ec_point_formats(11). The supported curves extension carries a NamedCurveList, whose items are ordered according to the client's preferences, favourite choice first. RFC 4492 defined 25 different curves in the NamedCurve registry, now renamed the TLS Supported Groups registry, of which only three had seen much use. This specification deprecates the rest, with numbers 1 to 22, and also deprecates the explicit curves with identifiers 0xFF01 and 0xFF02, and adds the new curves defined in RFC 7748. The curves that remain are secp256r1 with value 23, secp384r1 with value 24, secp521r1 with value 25, x25519 with value 29 and x448 with value 30. The named curves secp256r1, secp384r1 and secp521r1 are specified in SEC 2 and are also recommended in ANSI X9.62 and FIPS 186-4, and are referred to in the document as the NIST curves because they were originally standardised by the National Institute of Standards and Technology. The curves x25519 and x448 are defined in RFC 7748.

On point formats, three were included in the definition of ECPointFormat and this specification deprecates all but the uncompressed point format. Implementations MUST support the uncompressed format for all of their supported curves and MUST NOT support other formats for curves defined in this specification. The extension may still be included for backwards compatibility and contain exactly one value, the uncompressed point format, 0. If the client sends the extension and it does not contain the uncompressed point format, and the client has used the Supported Groups extension to indicate support for any of the curves defined in this specification, the server MUST abort the handshake and return an illegal_parameter alert.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the handshake can start, the client says which curves it can do, in the order it prefers. The server must then pick one the client can handle, or the handshake would fail later. The curve list has been trimmed hard: twenty-two old curves and two explicit ones are withdrawn, leaving three NIST curves and two newer ones. Only the uncompressed way of writing a point is allowed now.

sections.title: The Messages That Carry Elliptic Curve Data
sections.content:
The Server Certificate message is sent in all non-anonymous ECC-based key exchange algorithms and is used to authentically convey the server's static public key. For ECDHE_ECDSA the certificate MUST contain an ECDSA- or EdDSA-capable public key, and for ECDHE_RSA it MUST contain an RSA public key. If the client has used the Supported Elliptic Curves Extension, the public key in the server's certificate MUST respect the client's choice of curves, and a server that cannot satisfy this requirement MUST NOT choose an ECC cipher suite in its ServerHello. The client validates the certificate chain, extracts the server's public key, and checks that the key type is appropriate for the negotiated algorithm.

The Server Key Exchange message conveys the server's ephemeral ECDH public key and the corresponding curve domain parameters. The ECCurveType enum used to have values for explicit prime and explicit char2 curves, but those values are now deprecated and only named_curve (3) remains. The structure holding the parameters names a curve and carries the public key, and the curve type is sent as a byte string representation of an elliptic curve point. For the NIST curves the format is given again for convenience; for X25519 and X448 the only valid representation is the 32-octet or 56-octet representation of the u value of the point, and the structure MUST NOT be used with Ed25519 and Ed448 public keys.

On public key validation, with the NIST curves each party MUST validate the public key sent by its peer in the ClientKeyExchange and ServerKeyExchange messages. A receiving party MUST check that the x and y parameters from the peer's public value satisfy the curve equation, y squared equals x cubed plus a x plus b, modulo p. Failing to do so allows attackers to gain information about the private key, to the point that they may recover the entire private key in a few requests if that key is not really ephemeral. With X25519 and X448, a receiving party MUST check whether the computed premaster secret is the all-zero value and abort the handshake if so, as described in Section 6 of RFC 7748.
sections.plainLanguage: The server's certificate proves who it is, and the ServerKeyExchange carries the throwaway public key and the name of the curve. Both sides must check what they get back: for the NIST curves the coordinates have to lie on the curve, and for the newer curves the result must not be all zeros. Skipping the check lets an attacker learn the private key.

sections.title: The Cipher Suites
sections.content:
The document defines ECC cipher suites that use the key exchange algorithms. For ECDHE_ECDSA there are six: TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_NULL_SHA with identifier 0xC0, 0x06, TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA with 0xC0, 0x08, TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA with 0xC0, 0x09, TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA with 0xC0, 0x0A, TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 with 0xC0, 0x2B and TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 with 0xC0, 0x2C. For ECDHE_RSA there are six more: TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_NULL_SHA with 0xC0, 0x10, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA with 0xC0, 0x12, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA with 0xC0, 0x13, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA with 0xC0, 0x14, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 with 0xC0, 0x2F and TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 with 0xC0, 0x30. For ECDH_anon there are four: TLS_ECDH_anon_WITH_NULL_SHA with 0xC0, 0x15, TLS_ECDH_anon_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA with 0xC0, 0x17, TLS_ECDH_anon_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA with 0xC0, 0x18 and TLS_ECDH_anon_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA with 0xC0, 0x19.

The key exchange method, cipher and hash algorithm for each of these cipher suites are easily determined by examining the name. Server implementations SHOULD support all of TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, and client implementations SHOULD support at least one of them.

The document also records the implementation status: both ECDHE and ECDSA with the NIST curves are widely implemented and supported in all major browsers and all widely used TLS libraries, ECDHE with Curve25519 is implemented in several browsers and several TLS libraries including OpenSSL, and Curve448 and EdDSA have working interoperable implementations but are not yet as widely deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: A cipher suite is just a name that packs together the key exchange, the bulk cipher and the hash. This document lists sixteen of them for the elliptic curve algorithms, and then names four that both ends should implement.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security issues are discussed throughout the memo, and for TLS handshakes using ECC cipher suites the security considerations in Appendix D of each of the three TLS base documents apply accordingly. Security discussions specific to ECC can be found in IEEE P1363 and ANSI X9.62.

One important issue that implementers and users must consider is elliptic curve selection. Beyond elliptic curve size, the main issue is elliptic curve structure. As a general principle, it is more conservative to use elliptic curves with as little algebraic structure as possible, so random curves are more conservative than special curves such as Koblitz curves, and curves over F_p with p random are more conservative than curves over F_p with p of a special form, and curves over F_p with p random are considered more conservative than curves over F_2^m, as there is no choice between multiple fields of similar size for characteristic 2.

Another issue is the potential for catastrophic failures when a single elliptic curve is widely used, because an attack on the elliptic curve might then result in the compromise of a large number of keys. This concern may need to be balanced against the efficiency and interoperability improvements associated with widely used curves. The introduction of RFC 8032 lists the security, performance and operational advantages of EdDSA signatures over ECDSA signatures using the NIST curves. All of the key exchange algorithms defined in this document provide forward secrecy, while some of the deprecated key exchange algorithms do not.
sections.plainLanguage: The hard question is which curve to trust. A curve with extra algebraic structure is more likely to have an undiscovered weakness, so the RFC prefers the plainest ones. The other worry is popularity: if everybody uses the same curve, one break would affect everyone at once.

messages.label: CLIENT HELLO
messages.note: The client offers the ECC cipher suites, and the curves and point formats it supports.

messages.label: SERVER HELLO
messages.note: The server picks a curve the client can handle and a cipher suite to match.

messages.label: CERTIFICATE AND SERVER KEY EXCHANGE
messages.note: The certificate identifies the server. The key exchange carries the server's ephemeral public key and the curve, signed.

messages.label: CLIENT KEY EXCHANGE
messages.note: The client sends its own ephemeral public key on the same curve.

messages.label: FINISHED
messages.note: Both sides now hold the same premaster secret, and the master secret is derived from it.
